questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Parametrization of a Surface of Revolution: Rotation About the y-Axis or z-Axis
questions.problem:
$$
r(y,\theta )=⟨{e}^{1-{y}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y,\,\text{_______}⟩
$$

The vector-valued function $r(y,\theta )$ above parametrizes the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $x={e}^{1-{y}^{2}}$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis for $y\in [\frac{1}{2},2].$ What is the third component of $r?$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14081523/assets/be6fb27c0d050a7007e9f4a0d526daaff40b8f7d01f20c63ac8cc00074121f28.png)

 

A point $(x,y,z)$ on the surface generated by rotating the graph of $x=f(y)$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis has the position vector

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨f(y)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y,\,f(y)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,y\in [a,b],\,\theta =[0,2\pi ).\end{aligned}
$$

First, notice that $x=f(y)={e}^{1-{y}^{2}}\ge 0$ for all $y\in [\frac{1}{2},2].$ 

So, the parametrization of our surface of revolution is 

$$
r(y,\theta )=⟨{e}^{1-{y}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y,\,{e}^{1-{y}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,y\in [\frac{1}{2},2],\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

  

Therefore, the third component of $r$ is ${e}^{1-{y}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$

questions.knowledge_point: The Fundamental Vector Product of a Surface of Revolution
questions.problem:
$$
⟨\,(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\text{_______}\,,\,(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩
$$

 

The fundamental vector product of the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $x=1-\operatorname{cos}⁡y$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis for $y\in [0,\pi ]$ is given above. What is the $2$nd component of the product?
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that $x=1-\operatorname{cos}⁡y\ge 0$ for all $y\in [0,\pi ].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨f(y)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,y,\,f(y)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,(y,\theta )\in D\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(y)=1-\operatorname{cos}⁡y,$ and 

$$
D={(y,\theta )\,:\,0\le y\le \pi ,\,0\le \theta <2\pi }.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{y}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂y},\,\frac{∂y}{∂y},\,\frac{∂z}{∂y}⟩=⟨{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,1,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0,\,f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{y}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0 & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-{f}^{′}f{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{f}^{′}f{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-{f}^{′}f,\,f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f=1-\operatorname{cos}⁡y,$ we obtain ${f}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡y.$ So, finally, we conclude that the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{y}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}=⟨(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡y(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡y),\,(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
$$
⟨\,\text{_______}\,,\,-(x-2)^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,,\,-(x-2)^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩
$$

 

The fundamental vector product of the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $y=(x-2)^{2}$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis for $x\in [0,2]$ is given above. What is the $1$st  component of the product?
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that $y=(x-2)^{2}\ge 0$ for all $x\in [0,2].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is  

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨x,f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,(x,\theta )\in D\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(x)=(x-2)^{2},$ and  

$$
D={(x,\theta )\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,0\le \theta <2\pi }.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂x},\,\frac{∂y}{∂x},\,\frac{∂z}{∂x}⟩=⟨1,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨0,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨f{f}^{′}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +f{f}^{′}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨f{f}^{′},\,-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f=(x-2)^{2},$ we obtain ${f}^{′}=2(x-2).$ So, finally, we conclude that the fundamental vector product is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}=⟨2(x-2)^{3},\,-(x-2)^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-(x-2)^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Use a fundamental vector product to determine which of the following integrals gives the surface area generated when the curve $x={y}^{3}+1$ is rotated by $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis for $y\in [0,1].$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that $x={y}^{3}+1\ge 0$ for all $y\in [0,1].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨f(y)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y,\,f(y)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,(y,\theta )\in D\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(y)={y}^{3}+1,$ and

$$
D={(y,\theta )\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{y}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂y},\,\frac{∂y}{∂y}\,\frac{∂z}{∂y}⟩=⟨{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,1,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0,\,f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{y}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0 & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f{f}^{′}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -f{f}^{′}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f{f}^{′},\,f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{y}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖ & =\sqrt{(f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-f{f}^{′})^{2}+(f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}+{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}} \\  & =f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{y}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖\text{d}y\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{D}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(y)={y}^{3}+1,$ we obtain ${f}^{′}(y)=3{y}^{2}.$ So, finally, we conclude that our expression for the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}y & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{3}+1)\sqrt{1+(3{y}^{2})^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{3}+1)\sqrt{1+9{y}^{4}}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Use a fundamental vector product to determine which of the following integrals gives the surface area generated when the curve $y={e}^{x}(x-1)$ is rotated by $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis for $x\in [2,3].$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that $y={e}^{x}(x-1)\ge 0$ for all $x\in [2,3].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨x,\,f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,(x,\theta )\in D\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(x)={e}^{x}(x-1),$ and

$$
D={(x,\theta )\,:\,2\le x\le 3,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂x},\,\frac{∂y}{∂x},\,\frac{∂z}{∂x}⟩=⟨1,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨0,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨f{f}^{′}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +f{f}^{′}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨f{f}^{′},\,-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖ & =\sqrt{(f{f}^{′})^{2}+(-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}+{f}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}+{f}^{2}} \\  & =f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{D}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{3}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{3}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{2}^{3}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(x)={e}^{x}(x-1),$ we obtain ${f}^{′}(x)=x{e}^{x}.$ So, finally, we conclude that our expression for the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi {\int }_{2}^{3}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =2\pi {\int }_{2}^{3}{e}^{x}(x-1)\sqrt{1+(x{e}^{x})^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{2}^{3}{e}^{x}(x-1)\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}{e}^{2x}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$
